title: Technology in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about technology and the way we live and work with it: AI at work and at university, time online, energy, and who is still offline.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Our gut runs ahead of the data.
paras: On several of today's questions, the confident guess and the evidence parted company: the results for new tools were mixed, and some numbers have grown faster than anyone noticed.
Technology changes quickly; good evidence about it arrives more slowly. Both matter when decisions are made.

questions.q: In a 2025 study, 16 experienced software developers worked on 246 real tasks, some with AI coding tools allowed and some without. With AI, they were...
questions.explain: The developers took 19% longer when AI tools were allowed. Before the study they predicted AI would make them 24% faster, and afterwards they still believed it had made them about 20% faster. The researchers stress that the result may not apply to other kinds of work.

questions.q: In a 2025 survey of full-time UK undergraduates, what share said they use AI tools in some form in their studies?
questions.explain: Use jumped from 66% to 92% in a single year, and 88% said they had used generative AI such as ChatGPT for assessed work. The most common uses were explaining ideas, summarising articles and suggesting research topics.
questions.source: HEPI and Kortext, Student Generative AI Survey 2025

questions.q: In 2025, what share of German companies with ten or more employees used some form of artificial intelligence?
questions.explain: About a quarter of German companies used AI, above the EU average of 20% (up from 13.5% in 2024). Denmark was highest in the EU, at about 42%. The most common use was analysing written text, reported by about 12% of EU companies.

questions.q: The International Energy Agency estimates how much of the world's electricity data centres use. What was their share in 2024?
questions.explain: Data centres used about 415 terawatt-hours, around 1.5% of global electricity. The IEA expects that to more than double by 2030, to about 945 TWh, slightly more than Japan uses today, with AI the main driver.
questions.source: International Energy Agency (IEA), Energy and AI, 2025

questions.q: About 6 billion people used the internet in 2025. How many people still didn't?
questions.explain: Around three-quarters of the world is online, but 2.2 billion people are not. The gap is widest between town and country (85% of urban residents online, 58% in rural areas) and between rich and poor countries: in low-income countries only about 23% are online.
questions.source: International Telecommunication Union (ITU), Facts and Figures 2025

questions.q: Ofcom measures how long UK adults spend online each day, mostly on personal devices rather than for work. For 18- to 24-year-olds in 2025, what was the daily average?
questions.explain: Young adults spent 6 hours 20 minutes a day online. The average for all adults was 4 hours 30 minutes, ten minutes more than the year before, and 3 hours 20 minutes for those aged 65 and over. YouTube alone took 51 minutes a day.

questions.q: Economists studied more than 5,000 customer-support agents who were given an AI assistant. On average they solved 14% more problems per hour. For the newest, least experienced agents, the gain was...
questions.explain: Newer, less skilled agents improved by about 34%, while the most experienced barely improved at all: the tool seemed to pass on the habits of the best workers to everyone else. Customers' messages also became more positive, and fewer asked to speak to a manager.
questions.source: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 'Generative AI at Work', Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025

questions.q: In 2024 an employee of the engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong joined a video call with senior 'colleagues' who were all deepfakes, and made the transfers they asked for. How much?
questions.explain: The employee sent HK$200 million, about US$25 million, in 15 transfers after a call in which everyone else was an AI-generated fake. Arup confirmed that fake voices and images were used. It is one of the most widely reported deepfake frauds against a company.
questions.source: Hong Kong Police; Arup statement to CNN, May 2024
